glosses: Often followed by from, of, or out of: to free or release, or to rescue or save, (oneself or someone, or something).

examples.text: [Y]f there happen a plage of leproſy in any houſe of youre poſſeſſion, then ſhal he that ow[n]eth the houſe, come and tell the preſt, and ſaye: Methynke there is as it were a plage of leproſy in my houſe. glosses: To clear (a place or way); especially, to clear (land) of trees, undergrowth, etc.

examples.text: The vvaies […] Trajanius repaired, by paving vvith stone, or raiſing vvith banks caſt up ſuch peeces of them as vvere moiſt and miry; by ſtocking up & ridding ſuch as vvere rough and overgrovven vvith buſhes and briers: […]

glosses: Sometimes followed by away: to destroy or kill (someone).

examples.text: This Gloſter ſhould be quickly rid the VVorld, / To rid vs from the feare vve haue of him.

glosses: Sometimes followed by up: to remove obstacles or refuse from (a place); to clean, to clear out; specifically, to clear or empty (the stomach).

examples.text: Come, lads, drink up your ale, and we'll just rid this corner, so as to have all clear for beginning at the wall as soon as 'tis light to-morrow.

glosses: To settle (a disagreement).

glosses: To get away from or get out of (a place); to escape.

examples.text: We will make room for you! We will make a rid road from here to Winchester!

glosses: Progress which has been made; also, speed.

examples.text: Forkers are to bee foretolde that they give upp goode forkefulls [of hay], because the winde hath not soe much force and power to blowe it away, and likewise (by this meanes) it is sooner layde, and the loader comes more ridde.

glosses: Loose earth, rubble, etc., on the surface of a quarry which must be removed before digging can begin; rid-work.

examples.text: So Cupids faire mother be thy midvvife: out and alas I am mare rid, vvhat Somners Ghoſt or limme of Lucifer, puts poore Bordello in minde of pennance before he hath treſpaſſed?
